title: Effective sample size, dimensionality, and generalization in covariate shift adaptation
relevance: Shows importance weighting fails when the EFFECTIVE SAMPLE SIZE after reweighting collapses, and that this happens routinely as dimensionality rises. Gives us a go/no-go DIAGNOSTIC rather than an argument: fit a per-year density ratio, compute ESS, and if it collapses then weighted conformal (ID 124) cannot carry a guarantee to that year and we must fall back to the assumption-free penalty of Barber 2023 (ID 125). This is cheap, local, needs no labels, and should be run before any conformal design work.

authors: Fang, T., Lu, N., Niu, G. & Sugiyama, M.
title: Rethinking importance weighting for deep learning under distribution shift
source: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
relevance: Documents that classical importance weighting, which works for low-dimensional data and linear models, degrades on high-dimensional data with deep models, and proposes dynamic weight estimation instead of a fixed pre-computed ratio. Tempers the optimism of Search 19: the likelihood-ratio route is not a free lunch at image dimensionality, and a naive domain-classifier ratio is likely to saturate. Read alongside ID 124 before committing to weighted conformal as the spine of the deliverable.

authors: Serov, E., Koldasbayeva, D. & Zaytsev, A.
title: Kernel mean matching enhances risk estimation under spatial distribution shifts
relevance: Addresses the specific case we are in - SPATIALLY structured, clustered data - and reports that both no-weighting and classifier-based importance weighting fail there, because classifier-based weights inherit instability from imperfect separation and non-overlapping samples. Proposes kernel mean matching, which matches distribution means in a feature space instead of estimating a pointwise ratio, avoiding the high-variance step that breaks in high dimensions. This is the most plausible practical route to the reweighting that Search 19's guarantee depends on, and it is validated on spatial data rather than on benchmark tabular shifts.
